Tools and interfaces

Make tools that fit the person

The purpose running through these arrangements is to control complexity. You do not need to reproduce the author's computer, folders, or tool collection. Judge an arrangement by whether it reduces the burden of understanding, operation, and maintenance while retaining the capabilities you need. More tools and finer divisions of work do not automatically improve an environment.

One related software-engineering idea is a small, simple interface carrying deep, rich functionality. John Ousterhout's modular-design notes connect interface complexity, functionality, and information hiding. In a personal environment, “prepare reading material for this book” can be the person's entrance while the model locates editions, converts, organizes, and checks them. Sources, results, and consequential choices remain inspectable. “Small” concerns the operations and conventions a person must master; it does not require narrow natural-language purposes or impoverished content. Put complexity where it can be handled while keeping important choices visible.

The goal can be to entrust construction and maintenance of the whole daily working environment to the model: install and configure software, organize material, build tools, repair faults, maintain instructions and Skills, and connect the changes to daily use. The person primarily expresses purposes, reads, judges, and responds, writing only necessary Markdown. The model carries the remaining documents, code, configuration, and maintenance. It needs a clear work scope, usable tools, and resumable records; personal decisions such as purchases, identity verification, and publication remain governed by actual authorization.

Design separate entrances for the person and the model. The person needs native-language labels, clear hierarchy, clickable titles, and visible state and results. The model may work better with command-line interfaces, structured data, explicit tool contracts, and maintenance notes. Both entrances address the same work, with a maintained source rather than two copies the person must synchronize. Let the model connect tool choices and repeated steps it can resolve; present the choices that actually need human purpose, judgment, or authorization.

Configure search first and prefer existing tools

Use a hack-oriented approach of combining and adapting existing tools. Give the model working web and GitHub search and documentation access, verified with a real query. For a new need, first look for an existing implementation and inspect its documentation, recent maintenance, and user reports. Let the model install and configure it, arrange appropriate update checks, and adapt it through settings, plugins, small patches, or rewriting when necessary. Write a new implementation only when no suitable one exists. After updates, verify that the original work still succeeds and retain a recoverable version.

Several concrete search tools can be combined by purpose:

  • General web and source discovery: Brave Search searches webpages, news, and other information; Parallel, Exa, and Tavily offer search and information access for model use. Let the model select by source coverage and actual results rather than calling every service for each question.
  • Page reading and bulk extraction: Firecrawl reads pages, crawls sites, and extracts content. Discover the relevant object, then inspect the original. For recent community discussion, an available Last30Days integration can collect evidence across sources using a time range chosen for the question.
  • Papers and academic material: Consensus, SciSpace, and Hugging Face Papers are possible entrypoints, with Hugging Face Papers particularly close to the AI research ecosystem. Return to the paper, author, or publisher to check the original research.

These are examples rather than a list to purchase or install in full. Use an existing client's native search when sufficient; add a relevant plugin, MCP connection, or API when coverage, full-text access, or specialist sources are missing, and verify it with a real query. Several tools returning the same source do not provide several independent pieces of evidence.

Use other people's GitHub repositories

Give the model the repository link and the outcome you want. Have it read the README, installation instructions, license, and supported platforms before choosing an entrance:

  • Use a released tool: when the project supplies application installers or Releases, select the version for your operating system and processor. Command-line tools may instead use Homebrew, pip, or npm. A source ZIP is not necessarily a runnable application. GitHub's download guide distinguishes source snapshots from clones with history.
  • Run or study the source: to run source code, inspect implementation, or keep following updates, have the model clone the repository, prepare documented dependencies and configuration, and verify an example with real input. A downloaded ZIP generally omits Git history.
  • Adapt it to your needs: first judge whether configuration, a plugin, or a small patch is enough; fork when you need to maintain your own remote version. Keep the reason for changes, the upstream source, and a recoverable version. Compare local modifications with upstream changes during updates, resolve conflicts, and verify the result again.
  • Ask, contribute, and reuse: search existing Issues and documentation first. For a reproducible problem, collect the environment, steps, and result in an Issue; propose improvements through a PR. GitHub's contribution guide describes this path. The model can use GitHub CLI or a connected GitHub tool where useful, posting under your actual authorization. A repository may also supply papers, documentation, Skills, templates, or implementation ideas; its license determines the permitted copying and adaptation.

Connect actions with scripts, Hooks, Skills, and interfaces

A setting, direct link, or short script may be sufficient. When a method needs repeated use, access across projects, or distribution to others, choose an appropriate package:

  • Small script: connect concrete actions, such as turning materials into a linked reading page, providing a clearly named menu for common actions, or displaying a background task's completion and errors. The human entrance can be a button, menu, or webpage while the model maintains execution details.
  • Hook: connect an action to a defined event, such as checking formatting before a commit or recording a result afterward. Where a client exposes the relevant events, a Hook can also organize tool output or display a task-completion notification. Git hooks are one concrete example. Events, inputs, and failure handling belong to the actual host; one client's configuration cannot simply be copied into another. Have the model connect the existing entrypoint, trigger a real event, and inspect the result, so the action does not depend only on a prompt saying to remember it.
  • Skill: describe a recurring task's purpose, method, required material, and checks in a capability package the model loads when needed. Agent Skills can include instructions, scripts, references, and templates. Their value is making the next task resumable, not accumulating files.
  • MCP: use Model Context Protocol when a model needs a stable interface to a data source or operation. Examples include querying a reading catalog, reading selected notes, or calling an existing conversion program. Scope access and write capabilities to the actual work.
  • Plugin: where the selected client supports it, package related Skills, tool connections, and resources for installation, discovery, and updates. Packaging depends on the client; a useful local script does not first have to become an MCP server or plugin.

From public Skills to your own tools

You can start with a public Skill and ask a model to adapt and maintain it for your actual work. These are public sources to explore; some projects may be preserved in full, while others contribute only a subdirectory or individual Skill, sometimes with local adaptations. This source list does not mean every repository or every file in it is installed.

Area Public sources and what they offer
Science and decisions K-Dense Scientific Agent Skills: scientific workflows and databases; HowToLiveBetter: source-backed life decisions with evidence grades.
Programming and engineering Superpowers: software development methods; Anthropic Skills: reusable task capabilities; Matt Pocock Skills and Addy Osmani Agent Skills: engineering practice and code quality.
Models and context Hugging Face Skills: the Hugging Face model and data ecosystem; Context Engineering Skills: context management and agent systems; TypeSafe Skills: composing structured judgments with TypeSafe.
Research, browsing, and diagrams Last30Days: recent research across communities; Jev Browser Use: text judgments that support browser actions; Diagram Design and Archify: diagrams and interactive architecture maps.
Tool creation CLI Creator in OpenAI Skills: package an existing interface or program as a composable command-line tool; this links to that one directory.

Your own Skills, scripts, and interfaces can take shape around real work. The reusable Skill catalog includes the draw wheel, research, teaching, papers and subtitles, singing, Android control, shopping, instruction audits, and environment maintenance. Each page identifies its Skill by a Chinese name and native English identifier. Package guides declare companion Skills and actual tools; download the needed group while preserving useful responsibilities. MCP servers and connected apps can be equally concrete: Jev MCP offers text-judgment tools, Logic Pro MCP connects to music software and reads project state, and PhotoCraft provides image-editing capability. The Google Drive app can find and work with cloud files within granted access, while ChatGPT Sites can create, preview, and publish websites. These are optional examples; choose tools for the task at hand.

Scripts can also support concrete daily actions. On Mac, ask the model to wrap a selected organization, checking, or synchronization script in a LaunchAgent, running after login, on a schedule, or under a suitable trigger and leaving inspectable results. Design keyboard shortcuts for frequent actions, such as opening working materials, translating selected text, or starting and stopping a recording. Check key conflicts and the active application, then connect the actions to existing habits. An AI input method can turn speech into text, add punctuation, organize expression, or support mixed Chinese and English input; verify the result in the actual input field. These tools shorten the distance from an idea to expression and action, while the model can carry configuration and maintenance.

Other practical tool ideas include: turn PDFs into readable material while preserving formulas and sources; connect selection translation to the current reading action; replace hard-to-remember commands with a searchable menu; link works, originals, and versions directly; and report meaningful background completion or failure while preserving the person's current window, input focus, and work. These are examples to select by the problem, not a required installation checklist.

Generate images, explain with diagrams, and edit images

Let the model select the visual form for the actual question. Image generation can produce illustrations, characters, atmosphere, and visual alternatives from a description; inspect whether exact numbers, relationships, or wording retain their meaning. Visual explanation can use Archify for explorable architecture, process, and state diagrams, and Diagram Design for concepts, comparisons, and relationships. Interactive pages can let readers change conditions and observe results. These tools and methods have their own upstream maintainers, instructions, and licenses.

Editing an existing image can use PhotoCraft: have the model open the selected image, inspect available operations, edit, preview, and export. Generating an image, explaining a relationship, and editing an original serve different purposes. Choose through what you need to understand or create. For study material, place key objects, arrow meanings, conditions, and source support beside the diagram so it contributes to understanding rather than decoration alone.

Organize work across life with Skills and Projects

This approach can serve many areas of life: psychological exploration and organizing experience, shopping comparisons, coursework, preparing for medical appointments and reading medical material, work projects, game setup and guides, exercise records and plans, and music listening, recording, and practice. Different domains need different knowledge, evidence, and professional support. A model can help select and develop suitable methods, then connect the tools actually available.

A Skill preserves a reusable method, a Project organizes a continuing purpose with its materials and results, and tools perform concrete operations. A shopping Skill can serve different purchases, while a continuing study Project retains courses, progress, and exercises. A music project can connect singing practice, recording software, and earlier works. A Project may be a client's project feature or a workspace of local folders, documentation, and versions. Actual purposes, existing understanding, and use feedback supply a shared orientation while methods develop within their domains. Handle simple questions directly; let recurring or sustained work accumulate into Skills and Projects that can be continued.

Reading, terminals, and Vim-style controls

  • Browser: extensions such as Vimium bring Vim-style actions to webpages: j / k scroll, f displays link hints to open links, / searches the page, and H / L move backward or forward in history. They also support searching and switching tabs. Let the model select an extension for the actual browser, configure common bindings and site exclusions, and check reading pages, forms, and frequently used sites. Supported pages and input-field state affect the keys; successful installation alone does not establish useful operation.
  • Obsidian: read and edit necessary Markdown while the model maintains related material, links, and structure. It has reading and editing views, with built-in Vim bindings available directly in the editor; basic Vim editing does not first require a community plugin. Reading-mode navigation, tab switching, and plugin actions need their own configuration and checks. If an actual action exceeds the built-in capabilities, let the model assess suitable plugins and their current compatibility.
  • IDEs and code editors: use VSCodeVim in VS Code or IdeaVim in JetBrains IDEs to bring Vim modes, movement, and editing habits into the existing editor. Completion, debugging, project navigation, and other commands remain IDE capabilities. Let the model configure which keys each handles and check conflicts while editing, completing, and debugging a real project; consistent controls do not require replacing the whole IDE.
  • Sioyek: read textbook and paper PDFs with their original layout, using its navigation, search, and marks to move through material. The model can prepare reading entrances, configure controls, and link citations to actual files.
  • cmux: organize terminals and model tasks into recognizable workspaces. Its vertical tabs, split panes, and programmable interfaces make task names and status visible.
  • Editing and command lines inside a terminal: Vim / Neovim edit files; a shell's Vi mode edits commands before execution. These are separate entrances. In zsh, begin with built-in bindkey -v; consider the zsh-vi-mode plugin when more complete Vim-style command editing serves an actual need. Let the model inspect the current shell, completion, and history search, then test entering, changing, executing, and recovering commands after configuration. Terminal tabs, panes, and scrollback remain separately managed by the terminal application.

Let the model align common movement, search, history, tab, and pane actions with Vim-style habits across applications. An editor's Vim mode, PDF navigation, and terminal workspaces are different capabilities; test conflicts and actual effects rather than delivering only a shortcut table. Retain mouse controls, native-language labels, and searchable menus. Vim-style operation should preserve familiar actions and reduce switching costs.

Arrange the UI: vertical navigation with important work near the top

For interfaces with multiple pages, documents, or tasks, prefer available vertical tabs, lists, or sidebars. Group work by purpose, use recognizable names, and keep related materials and tasks together. Put important, frequent, and current work near the top, pinning it where supported. Collapse or archive infrequent items, rather than letting a default “recently updated” order continually direct your attention.

Interface Possible arrangements
Codex Organize work through the left-hand vertical task list and project groups; use the current version's available pinning, ordering, and archiving features to make priority tasks easy to return to.
Chrome Use vertical tabs, a sidebar, or tab groups available in the current version to keep pages for the same purpose together; put frequent entrances first and collapse groups not currently needed.
Obsidian Use sidebar Bookmarks for frequent notes, groups, and ordering; use Workspaces to retain a task's open files, tabs, and sidebar layout.
Web ChatGPT Organize sidebar conversations and Projects, using clear project names to bring related work together; use available pinning, ordering, or archiving features to keep priorities visible.

Let the model configure the features the actual application provides, applying the same principles to websites and tools you create. Allow sidebars to collapse and change width, closing them on narrow screens to leave room for content. Check the arrangement through a real task: can you recognize important work, reach related material, and return to where you were? Revise through use without making every application adopt identical controls for a similar appearance.

Consolidate global configuration with chezmoi

Let the model establish a Git-managed global configuration repository and use chezmoi to bring terminal, editor, keyboard, script-entry, and reconstructible model settings under a maintained source. The model edits source, inspects differences, applies changes, and reads back their effects in the actual applications. GitHub preserves versions for ongoing maintenance, migration, and recovery. Consolidate configuration ownership without putting all application data into one repository: passwords, tokens, login sessions, caches, and temporary state keep their appropriate owners.

Give multiple Obsidian vaults one shared base configuration: maintain themes, plugin selection, common settings, and Vim mappings centrally, then let the model synchronize them across vaults. Notes remain in their own vaults, and necessary vault-specific differences remain explicit. Cloud-backed and ordinary local directories may need different copying or linking mechanisms; the model chooses the appropriate method and checks what each open vault actually loads. This reduces repeated setup without allowing a shared configuration update to overwrite note contents.

Start with a request such as: “I do this often, but currently have to remember several commands and switch windows. Inspect the existing approach and give me an entrance I can understand, retaining the result location, failure feedback, and recovery. Try it through once.” Let the model implement and verify the change. Check whether the person can complete the work from that entrance and recover after an error; code executing successfully is only part of that result.
